article.articleHeadline: Vietnamese sailor dies in Chile due to imported malaria.
article.articleSummary:
- Imported malaria caused the death of a Vietnamese merchant seaman who arrived aboard the NV Athena from Singapore and was hospitalized in Talcahuano, Biobío Region, Chile. He died after admission to Las Higueras Hospital with hemorrhagic fever. Chile’s Public Health Institute confirmed malaria by laboratory testing and ruled out Ebola. Regional Health Secretary Isabel Rojas stated that malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes carrying Plasmodium, and there is no malaria transmission in Biobío, so there is no contagion risk to the rest of the crew; quarantine was lifted and the vessel was allowed to continue sailing. This incident underscores the importation risk of malaria and confirms no local transmission in this case.
- Malaria diagnosed in a Vietnamese merchant seaman who died in Talcahuano, Biobío Region, Chile. Diagnosis confirmed by the Instituto de Salud Pública after Hospital Las Higueras sent clinical samples. The sailor arrived on a merchant vessel from Singapore and, due to severe illness, the ship diverted to Talcahuano for urgent care; he died the night before. Seremi de Salud de la Región del Biobío, led by Isabel Rojas, stated there is no epidemiological risk to port workers or the local population. Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes carrying Plasmodium, a vector not present in Biobío. Consequently, infection risk to the remaining crew is zero, and the vessel’s preventive quarantine was lifted, allowing the ship to continue to its next port.

The vessel had arrived from Singapore and was near Tomé, Punta de Parra, with indications the illness may have arisen during a stop in Africa. Samples were sent to the Institute of Public Health (ISP); Ebola was ruled out and other diagnoses awaited. ISP later confirmed malaria as the diagnosis. The ship’s 21 crew members were quarantined while investigations proceeded. The malaria parasite Plasmodium is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, not present in Biobío region, leading authorities to deem the crew’s risk as low and to lift free pratique, allowing the vessel to proceed to its next port.

article.articleHeadline: The UN warned of the risk of a new HIV epidemic.
article.articleSummary:
- UNAIDS warns that shrinking international funding for HIV programs in low- and middle-income countries threatens recent gains and risks a renewed epidemic. In 2025, global HIV financing declined to $7.3 billion from $8.8 billion in 2024, an 18% drop—the largest reduction in nearly two decades. Prevention, testing, and treatment programs have already felt the impact. In Cameroon, Nigeria, and Zambia, more than 50% fewer people received HIV prevention services. New infections are rising in 21 countries. Globally, about 1.2 million people were infected with HIV in 2025, and AIDS-related deaths totaled around 570,000. By 2024, approximately 9 million of the 41 million people living with HIV worldwide did not receive treatment. UNAIDS warns of renewed spread if funding does not rebound.

A report cited by TASS shows international HIV financing in low- and middle-income countries fell 18% last year, from $8.8 billion to $7.3 billion—the largest drop in nearly two decades. Cutbacks have eroded prevention, testing, and treatment services; Cameroon, Nigeria, and Zambia each saw more than a 50% drop in people receiving HIV prevention. Despite tighter resources, new HIV infections are rising in 21 countries. Separately, Chile declared alarm over a new deadly virus, signaling another infectious-disease threat. The document urges renewed commitments and rapid action to avert reversing decades of progress in global HIV control.

Last year, low- and middle-income countries reduced HIV program funding by $1.5 billion (18%), the largest budget cut in 20 years. Africa is the first to be affected, with Cameroon, Nigeria, and Zambia among the hardest hit. The report also flags 21 countries showing rising new HIV infections. From 2010 to 2025, growth occurred in Eastern Europe and Central Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East and North Africa. In the last year, HIV infections were identified in 1.2 million people, with 570,000 deaths; roughly 9 million people living with HIV were not receiving treatment. Without renewed commitments, the world risks a renewed HIV surge.

Progress under the Malaria Elimination Roadmap 2025–2045 includes TOKEN, Mass Drug Administration, Targeted Drug Administration, and Intermittent Preventive Treatment for at-risk groups. - Malaria in Sorong City, Southwest Papua, Indonesia, shows 1,509 confirmed cases from January–June 2026, out of 32,547 tested (77% of the 42,427 target). Of positives, 1,324 patients (87.7%) received treatment per standard guidelines. Highest incidence is in Maladumes, Sorong Barat, Sorong Manoi, and Sorong Kepulauan districts, guiding control efforts. Annual Parasite Incidence (API) is 4.90 per 1,000 population, above the elimination target of <1 per 1,000. To accelerate elimination, the Sorong City Health Office is conducting a malaria elimination socialization involving regional government agencies and stakeholders to strengthen cross-sector collaboration. Officials aim for malaria-free Sorong by 2028–2029, aligning with Indonesia’s national elimination target for 2030.

article.articleHeadline: Snake venom breaks the resistance of the schistosome parasite.
article.articleSummary: Researchers from the University of São Paulo and the Butantan Institute tested venoms from eight Bothrops snakes on Schistosoma mansoni, which causes visceral schistosomiasis in Latin America and Africa, assessing effects on gene expression and reproduction. Some venoms reduced locomotion, attachment, viability, and disrupted egg-laying; moojeni venom was most potent, nearly abolishing egg deposition and markedly impairing movement, while jararacuçu reduced egg laying. After incubation, male and female worms were sequenced separately, revealing a systemic collapse in males with many more genes affected than in females. Affected male genes relate to cell division and nerve signal transmission, whereas female changes pertain more to reproductive processes. The study highlights non-coding RNAs as potential therapeutic targets. Praziquantel remains the only approved drug, raising concerns about resistance. Future work aims to design synthetic molecules to target these RNAs and test them in vivo and in clinical trials, per International Journal of Molecular Sciences.

article.articleHeadline: A Historic Milestone for Brazilian Livestock Farming: Brazil Inaugurates the National Antigen Bank and Expands Biosecurity Against Foot-and-Mouth Disease

It strengthens rapid response, surveillance, and preparedness, aligned with the National Plan for Surveillance for Foot-and-Mouth Disease (PNEFA). The project underscores government-science-private sector cooperation, with Biogénesis Bagó bringing over three decades of international FMD experience. Attendees included Agriculture Minister André de Paula, underscoring the instrument’s significance for global livestock health and trade security.

article.articleHeadline: Lagoon that went viral in Pará raises alarm over potential unseen risks.
article.articleSummary: Crystal-clear lagoon in Vigia de Nazaré, Pará, Brazil, has drawn swarms of bathers but lacks official water-quality data, triggering public health concern. Investigations suggest the site may have formed in a former sand-mining area, possibly influenced by an old landfill, raising worries about inorganic contaminants. Experts warn that water clarity does not equal safety; lab analyses are essential to identify contaminants, including toxic elements like mercury, arsenic, and lead, and to determine balneability. Authorities—environment and health secretariats—should publish examinations and monitor conditions; Brazil’s Conama resolutions govern water-body classification and permitted recreational use. Mining-related contamination could involve heavy metals; rainfall may mobilize them into waters. Sewage discharges pose another major hazard, as fecal coliforms indicate contamination and could transmit diseases such as hepatitis and cholera. Until official assessments confirm bathing safety, residents should rely on approved studies and official guidance before swimming.

article.articleHeadline: Avian Influenza in Antarctica: Risks for Brazil.
article.articleSummary: H5N1 Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza has reached Antarctica, per DigiVets Brochure No. 10 by Prof. Masaio Mizuno Ishizuka. The first isolation was on James Ross Island in a brown skua (Stercorarius antarcticus), classified as clade 2.3.4.4b linked to South American lineages. Predatory and scavenging seabirds—skuas, petrels, albatrosses—likely introduced the virus, traveling between Chile, Argentina, subantarctic islands, and the Antarctic. The Antarctic fauna, with dense breeding colonies and possible low herd immunity, faces elevated transmission risk; emperor penguins may suffer profound ecological impacts. For Brazil, risks relate to Southern Cone routes and marine birds connecting the region to the Brazilian coast (South and Southeast). Surveillance is essential, particularly Sept–Dec migratory period (peak Oct–Nov), focusing on mangroves, estuaries, coastal islands, ports, and lagoon areas. A May 2025 H5N1 outbreak on a commercial farm in Montenegro, Rio Grande do Sul is noted; no subsequent cases in 2025; reinforces need for risk analysis and field monitoring.

article.articleHeadline: Livestock producers must vaccinate the herd against brucellosis in the state of Mato Grosso do Sul - Mato Grosso do Sul State Government News Agency
article.articleSummary: Brucellosis vaccination campaign in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil is in its second stage (July 1–December 31, 2026) under Iagro, the state animal and vegetal health surveillance agency. The vaccination is mandatory for all female cattle and buffaloes aged 3–8 months, with registration in the e-Saniagro system required by December 31, 2026 for the vaccine to be considered valid. Noncompliance can lead to fines, movement restrictions of animals, sanitary actions, and potential economic losses. It reinforces One Health priorities—protecting animal health, food safety, and public health.

article.articleHeadline: What is malaria and how is it transmitted? What you need to know about the disease that caused the death of a Vietnamese crew member in Chile.
article.articleSummary: Malaria, an acute febrile illness caused by Plasmodium and transmitted mainly by female Anopheles mosquitoes, caused the death of a Vietnamese crew member in Talcahuano, Chile. The patient arrived at Hospital Las Higueras after the vessel requested an emergency port call; authorities lifted the ship’s health quarantine as no risk to the rest of the crew. Chile has had no autochthonous malaria cases since 1945; all national cases are imported, with a notable rise since 2010. In Arica y Parinacota, the local vector is Anopheles (Anopheles pseudopunctipennis), and surveillance remains to prevent reestablishment. Prevention emphasizes bed nets, protective clothing, skin repellents, and chemoprophylaxis for travelers after medical consultation. Globally, most cases and deaths occur in Sub-Saharan Africa; in South America, Brazil, Colombia, and Venezuela account for higher incidence. The recent case underscores imported malaria risks in Chile and the importance of prevention and timely treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Hepatitis A up 250.4% in Minas Gerais in one year; rains in Juiz de Fora drive the rise.
article.articleSummary: Minas Gerais, Brazil records a 250.4% year‑on‑year rise in hepatitis A cases, with 1,654 infections from January to July 2026, vs. 472 in the same period in 2025 and 754 for all of 2025. The surge is driven largely by heavy rains in Juiz de Fora (Zona da Mata) suggesting waterborne transmission, while Belo Horizonte shows a persistent increase among men aged 20–40 linked to fecal‑oral sexual transmission. Sinan data indicate a March 2026 peak (451 cases), followed by a June decrease (108). One death occurred in Juiz de Fora in 2026; 2025 deaths totaled three in Belo Horizonte, Claraval, and Patos de Minas. Epidemiological investigation is ongoing, with the basic hypothesis being waterborne transmission; authorities are reinforcing vaccination in affected areas as part of public health response.

article.articleHeadline: Not Only Drought, BMKG Predicts Strong El Niño Through 2027, Posing a Risk of Triggering a New Outbreak.
article.articleSummary: Indonesia braces for a stronger El Niño through early 2027, with a 98% chance of moderate intensity and 62% chance of strong, triggering a drier, longer dry season. BMKG warns that extreme heat and air pollution will deteriorate urban air quality via PM2.5, elevating acute respiratory infections (ISPA) and heat-related illnesses such as heatstroke. Health expert Dicky Budiman notes broader impacts, including worsening cardiovascular disease risk, with PM2.5 exposure potentially triggering heavier asthma symptoms and accelerating COPD (Penyakit Paru Obstruktif Kronik) exacerbations due to systemic inflammation and coagulation. El Niño is described as a multiplier of health risk rather than a direct cause, amplifying environmental conditions that favor disease spread and outbreak potential. Fires from drought may further degrade air quality. BMKG Chief Teuku Faisal Fathani and researchers emphasize Indonesia's vulnerability through 2026–2027; no specific outbreaks are yet attributed to El Niño.

article.articleHeadline: Malaria cases remain a cause for concern; recognize the symptoms and the proper way to prevent it.
article.articleSummary: Malaria remains a public health challenge in Indonesia, with 346,866 cases recorded by July 2026; globally, 2024 data report 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths. Transmission occurs via infected female Anopheles mosquitoes and can spread through contaminated blood transfusions, shared needles, or mother-to-fetus transmission. Prevention emphasizes personal protection and environmental cleanliness to reduce mosquito breeding; travelers should consult a clinician beforehand for risk assessment and preventive measures; use mosquito repellent or prescribed prophylaxis, with attention to possible side effects; stay informed about malaria risks; limit outdoor activities, especially in the morning and late afternoon when mosquitoes are most active; pregnant women and children should avoid malaria-endemic areas. Symptoms typically appear 10–15 days after a bite, or months later, including high fever, headache, nausea/vomiting, weakness, chills, muscle/joint pain, and sweating; severe malaria may cause shortness of breath, jaundice, dark urine, severe anemia, or altered consciousness or seizures. Timely prevention is essential.

article.articleHeadline: Be vigilant for typhoid fever during the flood season.
article.articleSummary: Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella Typhi, poses heightened risk during flood season when water and food are easily contaminated. It typically presents with sudden high fever, headache, fatigue, loss of appetite, slow pulse, and either constipation or diarrhea; in some cases, symptoms are mild or absent. Incubation averages 8–14 days. Primary sources are infectious patients; recovered individuals who shed bacteria for 2–3 weeks after symptoms resolve, and, less clearly, asymptomatic carriers who may shed for 2–3 months. Transmission is via contaminated food or water and through direct contact with patients or carriers (feces, waste, dirty hands, contaminated objects). Prevention focuses on surveillance in high-risk, sanitation-limited areas; prompt reporting; clean water supply, waste management, food safety, and environmental hygiene; and public education on cooking, boiling water, and handwashing. Seek medical care for prolonged fever or digestive symptoms to diagnose and treat promptly and reduce spread; antibiotics are used to eradicate the bacteria and prevent complications and death.

article.articleHeadline: How many commune-level administrative units in Ninh Bình Province still have African swine fever and avian influenza outbreaks that have not yet passed the 21-day period?
article.articleSummary: In Ninh Bình Province, Vietnam, as of end-July 2026, 14 communes/wards still have African swine fever (ASF) outbreaks not yet past the 21-day clearance, and 7 communes/wards remain with avian influenza (AI) outbreaks not yet 21 days clear. Cumulatively from January 1 to July 27, 2026, authorities culled 9,673 pigs (about 530,983 kg) and 177,432 poultry (over 252 tonnes). A new AI outbreak was reported; only one AI outbreak has surpassed the 21-day safety window. The provincial government issued Directive 5173/UBND-VP3 to intensify vaccination, disinfection, surveillance, and strict enforcement, with daily reporting by local authorities and measures to prevent further spread and protect public health.

article.articleHeadline: Hepatitis and Coagulopathy Due to Chickenpox
article.articleSummary: A 32-year-old man from Vĩnh Long, Vietnam, treated at Can Tho City General Hospital for chickenpox complicated by pneumonia, severe respiratory failure, hepatitis, and coagulopathy. Three days before admission, vesicular skin eruptions appeared; by day four he deteriorated with purulent lesions. Varicella zoster virus (VZV) spreads via respiratory droplets and direct contact with vesicles, capable of disseminating to the liver, lungs, skin, and other organs. In adults, immune responses can be intense, raising liver enzymes and risking acute liver failure, especially with preexisting liver disease. Secondary bacterial infection by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A), or Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause cellulitis, abscess, bacteremia, septic shock, and multiorgan dysfunction. Prevention emphasizes hygiene and vaccination with varicella vaccine or the combined measles–mumps–rubella–varicella vaccine; masking when symptomatic or exposed. Zoster vaccination is advised for older adults or immunocompromised individuals.

article.articleHeadline: Timely vaccination prevents rabies early on.

A 59-year-old man sought vaccination within two hours after a dog bite; a dog-cat rescue worker notes frequent bites and consistently seeks medical advice before vaccination. Dr. Đinh Văn Thới stresses rabies is almost 100% fatal once symptoms appear but preventable with prompt vaccination, and warns against delaying care or using folk remedies. Health authorities (HCMC Department of Health, HCDC) are boosting surveillance and public education to curb animal-to-human transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Proactively blocking the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak at its source.
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) detected by proactive surveillance in Lao Cai Province, Vietnam, among apparently healthy cattle and buffalo at Coc Ly and Bac Ha markets. From June 30 to July 3, 68 blood and 68 throat-swab samples from 68 animals tested positive for FMD virus, types A and O; Coc Ly had 5 positives, Bac Ha 7. On July 10, 20 more samples from 9 high-risk households in Bao Nhai and Bac Ha yielded one additional positive, a type A in a buffalo, which was isolated. Authorities enacted synchronized control: vaccination, disinfection, temporary halt of livestock market activities, quarantine, and enhanced surveillance; 800 vaccine doses were received, with 312 cattle/buffalo vaccinated in Bac Ha. Movements now require vaccination-confirmation. Challenges include limited veterinary manpower. Early detection before clinical signs is crucial to limiting spread.

article.articleHeadline: Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome due to septic shock from biliary tract infection.
article.articleSummary: Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome from septic shock due to biliary tract infection in a 31-year-old Cambodian woman treated in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. After ERCP removed a common bile duct stone, she presented with severe abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, and hypotension (70/52 mmHg). MRI showed dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts with sludge; the gallbladder contained an ~11 mm stone. She required ICU support with fluids, vasopressors, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and blood cultures. After 24 hours, she stabilized and underwent a combined procedure: ERCP stone extraction and laparoscopic cholecystectomy in a single session. Intraoperative findings included a distal CBD stone ~18 mm and a large left hepatic duct stone; stones were fragmented and removed, ducts flushed, and a stent placed. A subsequent laparoscopic cholecystectomy used a fundus-first approach due to heavy inflammation; gallbladder contained 10–12 mm stones near the neck. Postoperative recovery improved; discharge after 5 days. Clinicians highlight gallstone complications—cholangitis, sepsis, biliary obstruction—and urge early recognition of RUQ pain, fever, and jaundice.

article.articleHeadline: No cough or fever, but weakness all over; an octogenarian man diagnosed with pneumonia.
article.articleSummary: As of July 29, 2026, an 80-year-old man in Zhejiang Province presented with non-specific symptoms—profound weakness, poor appetite, and lethargy—without cough or fever, later found to have severe bilateral pneumonia on chest CT. At Zhejiang Province Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine Hospital (Hangzhou Red Cross Hospital), he exhibited a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of 180 mg/L and a history of atrial fibrillation with a prostate tumor, marking his second pneumonia hospitalization within six months. The case underscores that elderly pneumonia often presents atypically due to blunted cough reflex and immune senescence, with rapid progression to heart or respiratory failure, sepsis, and electrolyte disturbances. Prevention emphasizes vaccination for those over 60 (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, RSV when indicated) and aspiration-prevention measures: upright meals, small, frequent feeds, high-protein nutrition, and delaying recumbency after eating. Families should seek prompt hospital evaluation for abrupt cognitive or appetite changes.

article.articleHeadline: Litong District Holds Tuberculosis Prevention and Control Knowledge Contest.
article.articleSummary: Litong District in Wuzhong City, Ningxia, China organized a tuberculosis prevention and control knowledge contest to test TB policies, professional knowledge, control skills, and health education. The event featured four rounds—individual, group, rapid-fire, and risk questions—covering TB transmission, contact screening timing, and management of multidrug-resistant TB. Participants cited applying casework from home visits, and the competition aims to promote learning, practice, and action in TB control. The district CDC coordinates a three-in-one service system with designated hospitals and primary and community clinics: the CDC provides coordination and technical guidance; the district hospital standardizes treatment; township hospitals supervise adherence and follow-up, with family doctors delivering home visits, counseling, nutrition support, and medication guidance. TB is included in rural poverty relief with a 'first diagnosis, then payment' policy and a triple protection scheme—basic medical insurance, major illness insurance, and medical assistance—plus information sharing among health, insurance, and civil affairs to aid eligible patients.

article.articleHeadline: ADLM: a blood test that rapidly detects up to 97% of tuberculosis infections.
article.articleSummary: Chinese molecular biologists have developed a blood-based test to rapidly and accurately detect pulmonary tuberculosis, achieving up to 97% accuracy by measuring the ESAT-6 protein in blood, thereby avoiding sputum collection and lengthy culture. Described by the press service of the International Association for Diagnostics and Laboratory Medicine (ADLM), the method could simplify and reduce the cost of mass TB screening. The test relies on ESAT-6, a protein secreted by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, whose levels rise with disease progression, helping explain its strong diagnostic performance compared with traditional host biomarker–based approaches. The researchers are linked to a Veterans’ Hospital in Taipei, Taiwan. As of 2026-07-29, this blood-based TB diagnostic approach shows potential for rapid, scalable detection and broader screening, with implications for public health diagnostics.

article.articleHeadline: Nanoparticles carrying Salmonella represent an effective anti-cancer therapy.
article.articleSummary: Attenuated Salmonella typhimurium engineered as a cancer-therapy carrier accumulates around tumors after radiotherapy in mice, enhancing anti-tumor immunity. Bacteria are coated with positively charged nanoparticles that capture negatively charged tumor antigens released by radiation, effectively packaging antigens for dendritic cells. In mouse experiments, this approach significantly boosts dendritic cell activity and increases interaction between tumor antigens and immune cells. The treated group showed an 83% survival rate, compared with 25% in a placebo control. The therapy was described as safe and effective in mice, though tumor–immune interactions differ between mice and humans. Lead researchers, including Jinhu Wu and colleagues at Nanjing University in China, plan further tests before human trials. The findings appeared in Nature Biomedical Engineering.

article.articleHeadline: UN: An HIV epidemic threatens the world.
article.articleSummary: UNAIDS warns of a renewed global HIV epidemic if development assistance and prevention funding keep shrinking. In 2025 international aid fell 23%, with net HIV funding down 18% to $7.3 billion from $8.8 billion—the lowest in two decades. In poor countries, external aid supported up to 90% of prevention activities. The report says reduced funding and scaled-back prevention and community programs could drive transmission: 1.2 million new infections and 570,000 AIDS-related deaths in 2025; without urgent action toward 2030, infections could exceed 3 million. New infections rose in three regions and 21 countries, including Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Condom procurement and services for key populations fell by 50–85%. A 2026 study in 47 countries found community prevention/treatment services cut by 50%, with 85% drops for MSM, 82% for sex workers, and 72% for survivors of gender-based violence. About 9 million of 41 million people living with HIV were untreated in 2025; nearly half of infected children lacked ART. In June, the UN warned of financial strain, with the US and China among top arrears. Czechia reported record HIV incidence linked to COVID-19 and the Ukraine conflict.

article.articleSummary: Tasrif Pharmaceutical, LLC received its second U.S. patent covering a proprietary panel of humanized monoclonal antibodies and antigen-binding fragments targeting the Poliovirus Receptor (CD155/PVR). The lead candidate, TSRF-786C IgG4 (S241P), is humanized using Abzena’s Composite Human Antibody (CHAb) platform. The expanded IP portfolio builds on Tasrif’s foundational U.S. patent and supports development of next-generation modalities that exploit CD155 binding, including antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), bispecifics, T-cell engagers, and cell therapies such as CAR-T and CAR-NK. Tasrif is pursuing national phase protection in Japan, Europe, Canada, Australia, and China from its PCT applications. This patent activity underscores efforts to advance poliovirus receptor–targeted therapeutics and broader CD155-targeted platforms.

article.articleHeadline: Study: Industrial Poultry Farming Promotes the Spread of a Dangerous Bacterium.
article.articleSummary: Industrial poultry farming accelerates the spread of Campylobacter, the world’s leading bacterial cause of diarrhea, and drives the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains. A genomic study (nearly 2,800 Campylobacter genomes) from chicken and wild birds across 30 countries, including the United Kingdom, United States, and China, covering 1979–2024, shows a ~100-fold rise in strain exchange between farmed chickens and wild birds since 1900 and identifies mutations linked to antibiotic resistance. Intensive production yields chickens at five weeks, creating a cauldron of bacterial evolution that promotes mixing and diversification. In the United Kingdom, 60–80% of infections are linked to contact with raw chicken. Proper cooking kills the bacterium, but cross-contamination via meat, produce, or utensils poses ongoing risk. No country-specific case counts or imported/exported cases are detailed in the article.

article.articleHeadline: Preparing now for the next deadly pandemic
article.articleSummary: More than 120 biological research laboratories in 30 countries conducted gain-of-function research, funded by American taxpayers, with SARS-CoV-2 likely originating in a Wuhan, China lab. article.articleHeadline: Africa's Ebola outbreak stabilizing in parts but has not yet peaked.
article.articleSummary: Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues active transmission of Ebola caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus. As of July 27, 2026, cumulative laboratory-confirmed cases reach 3,360 with 1,487 deaths, 597 recoveries, and 733 patients in isolation. The outbreak remains centered in Ituri and North Kivu in eastern DRC; remote districts, security challenges, and population movement hinder epidemiologic investigations, contact tracing, and logistics. There is no approved vaccine or specific therapy for Bundibugyo ebolavirus. WHO assesses global risk as low and regional risk as high, while surveillance, testing, and case-finding expand; a DRC biomedical research institute has begun a clinical trial to evaluate a post-exposure prophylaxis candidate for high-risk contacts. In Uganda, no new confirmed cases since late June; all hospitalized patients have recovered and are discharged, with a 42-day observation ongoing. Cross-border risk management advances involve Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, Burundi, and others, with support from Africa CDC, WHO, ICRC, MSF, and China’s medical teams.

article.articleHeadline: Climate change is redrawing the malaria map in Africa, study finds
article.articleSummary: Nature study quantifies climate change's historical and future impact on malaria in sub-Saharan Africa's children, where most cases and deaths occur. It finds malaria overall has risen slightly due to climate change, but current warm hotspots see suppression of transmission, with possible elimination in extremely hot Sahelian countries. In West Africa (Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Mali), malaria may fall about 5%; Niger, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, and Somalia could reach elimination. Cooler regions—southern Africa and high-elevation East Africa—face rising risk, with 5% increases in the Ethiopian highlands (Kenya, Burundi) and in Angola, Zambia, and northeast South Africa; by 2100, risk could rise 20% in the Rift Valley and coastal southern Africa. Limiting warming to 2°C could avert about 5 excess cases per 1,000 children in southern Africa, with larger gains in East African highlands. Adaptation and surveillance are essential to counter shifting malaria threats.

article.articleHeadline: Chickens at Risk in the Monsoon! Be Vigilant, or There Will Be Heavy Losses.
article.articleSummary: As of July 29, 2026, during the monsoon in Bilaspur district, humidity in poultry sheds promotes rapid spread of infections among flocks. Without regular cleaning or with damp litter, bacteria, viruses, and parasites proliferate, enabling quick transmission. The most at-risk diseases are infectious coryza (respiratory bacterial infection), coccidiosis, Newcastle disease (Ranikhet), chronic respiratory disease (CRD), and diarrhea. Early signs include reduced feed and water intake, lethargy, sneezing, nasal discharge, facial swelling, breathing difficulties, and thin or bloody diarrhea, with drooping feathers and reduced egg production indicating illness. Coryza and diarrhea pose the highest risk during rain. Prevention focuses on keeping sheds clean and dry, replacing wet litter, providing clean drinking water, avoiding moldy feed, ensuring ventilation, and separating sick birds. Vaccination, strict biosecurity, and veterinary-guided treatment are key to reducing losses.

article.articleSummary: Lyme disease threatens dogs in Bokaro, India during the monsoon, when higher humidity and rapid growth of grass and shrubs boost tick infestations. Dr. Anil of Bokaro Pindrajodda First Class Veterinary Hospital notes ticks carry Borrelia bacteria, causing Lyme disease. Affected dogs commonly present fever, weakness, reduced appetite, lethargy, lameness, and joint pain or swelling; if untreated, the infection can reach the kidneys and prove fatal in severe cases. Preventive measures for dog owners during monsoon include regular tick-repellent medications and thorough post-walk checks, especially around the ears, neck, between the paws, and other body parts. Maintain clean, dry living spaces and regularly trim surrounding grass and shrubs. Periodically clean dog beds and toys. Seek veterinary care promptly if severe symptoms appear to ensure timely treatment and pet safety.

article.articleHeadline: Scientists find a possible way to stop malaria from spreading inside the body - CNBC TV18
article.articleSummary: Malaria parasite Plasmodium could be blocked from multiplying inside the human body by inhibiting Aurora-related Kinase 1 (Ark1), a protein identified by a joint India-UK study. Researchers from Biotechnology Research and Innovation Council-National Institute of Immunology (BIRAC-NII) in Delhi and the University of Nottingham report Ark1 acts as a control switch for parasite cell division; blocking it may stop growth. Malaria is transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, with parasites first migrating to the liver, then entering red blood cells where they replicate, causing fever, chills, sweating, weakness and body pain. Current therapies rely on artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), but resistance is arising in some regions. If successful, Ark1-targeted drugs would offer a different mechanism. Malaria has afflicted humans for around 10,000 years, with sub-Saharan Africa bearing the highest burden; hundreds of thousands die annually, and roughly 40% of the world’s population is at risk.

article.articleHeadline: Rotavirus is on the rise in Mumbai! What steps should be taken to protect children from infections during the monsoon?
article.articleSummary: Rotavirus outbreak rising in Mumbai during the monsoon, with pediatric gastroenteritis presenting as diarrhea, dehydration, abdominal cramps, vomiting, and fever, predominantly in children. Over recent weeks, doctors report a surge in stomach-flu-like illness attributed to rotavirus. Transmission is fecal-oral, via direct or indirect contact; onset within 1–3 days. Diagnosis relies on stool testing (ELISA or PCR), which is expensive and requires rapid results; clinical differentiation from other diarrheas is challenging. There is no specific anti-rotavirus treatment; antibiotics or antivirals are ineffective. Management centers on oral rehydration solutions or saline. Vaccination is urged as a crucial preventive measure. Precautions include avoiding outside food for several weeks and sticking to clean, home-cooked meals; avoid raw items such as chutney or salads. Also, swimming can spread the virus; avoid letting children swim and guard against swallowing pool water. This Mumbai outbreak highlights the need for child-protection measures during the monsoon.

article.articleHeadline: Drug-resistant TB: treatment and prevention; cured after six months of treatment | Drug resistant TB treatment
article.articleSummary: Drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) now offers a six-month cure with the BPaLM regimen, at no cost in Kerala government facilities. The WHO Global TB Report 2025 records 10.7 million TB cases and 1.23 million deaths in 2024, TB a leading killer. India accounts for a quarter of global TB; RR-TB burden remains high, with around 150,000 cases and 164,545 treated. Kerala reports about 200 DR-TB cases annually. DR-TB arises from infection by a DR-TB patient or from resistance developing to first-line drugs due to incomplete treatment, interruptions, or improper regimens. Under NTEP, UDST via NAAT (CBNAAT/TrueNat) is freely available in all Kerala districts. The six-month BPaLM regimen uses four oral drugs daily, with over 85% cure. Kerala government hospitals provide free treatment; private centers may refer after confirmation. Close contacts should be tested; if no active TB, CyTB skin test and, if positive, TB preventive therapy. Isolation is not routinely required.

article.articleHeadline: In Gurugram, a rare fungal infection in the eye caused by bat droppings; doctors saved the sight.
article.articleSummary: In Gurugram’s Cyber City, Artemis Hospital clinicians diagnosed a rare ocular fungal infection: isolated orbital histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. A Gurugram woman presented with chronic red eye, irritation, and discomfort unresponsive to standard therapy. Biopsy confirmed Histoplasma capsulatum, a fungus typically found in soil contaminated with bat and bird droppings and usually affecting the lungs. Remarkably, the patient had a fully normal immune system, making orbital involvement exceedingly uncommon. A multidisciplinary team treated her with antifungal therapy for about one year, with dosage and duration tailored to response. After completion, the infection was controlled and vision was preserved. This case underscores that immunocompetent individuals can develop isolated ocular histoplasmosis, successfully managed with timely diagnosis and sustained antifungal treatment at Artemis Hospital, Gurugram.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue fear in Ajjarakadu Kadabettu Colony
article.articleSummary: Dengue fears have gripped Ajjarakadu Kadabettu Colony in Ajjarakadu Ward, Udupi district, amid reports of stagnant water and foul odor due to inadequate sanitation and drainage works. City authorities’ cleaning efforts are criticized as insufficient. On Tuesday, Congress leader Prasad Raj Kanchan visited the colony to assess the situation and urged the civic authorities to immediately resolve sanitation and drainage problems and to adopt necessary health precautions. Senior Congress colleagues, including Surendra Acharya, Dominic Mascarenhas, Suresh Shetty Bannanje, Prashanth Poojari, Sajjan Shetty Mulya, Sadananda Muly, Suresh Kumard, and Sharath Kundar, accompanied him. article.articleHeadline: Special vaccination drive in Uttar Pradesh schools in August; protection against diphtheria and measles.
article.articleSummary: Uttar Pradesh to run a dual vaccination drive in August 2026 to protect 5-16 year-olds against diphtheria and measles. Phase 1 (Aug 3-7) delivers TD/TDAP boosters (Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis) to 5-6, 10, and 16-year-olds (class I, V, and X–XI) with TDAP-2, TD-10, and TD-16 doses, targeting 50-75 children per session across all 75 districts. Phase 2 (Aug 18-28) administers MR (Measles-Rubella) vaccine as an additional dose to 5-10 year-olds, aiming 100-125 vaccinations per school daily. The campaign spans government, aided schools, madrasas, and anganwadi centers, with a nodal teacher per school and school microplans. Health and education departments will coordinate, aided by ASHA and Anganwadi workers to list eligible children and inform parents via assemblies and meetings. Digital monitoring will track progress on portals, ensuring timely, complete coverage and targeted follow-up for missed children.

article.articleHeadline: Thousands of ships stranded in the Strait of Hormuz could carry a biological invasion to the world's oceans.
article.articleSummary: More than 1,500 commercial ships stranded in the Persian Gulf after the Strait of Hormuz closure on February 28 pose a risk of a 'biological invasion superspreader event' that could disseminate invasive marine species worldwide when shipping resumes. Idle hulls foster growth of microbes, algae, barnacles, mollusks, and other invertebrates. As trade reopens, these organisms could hitchhike to ports globally, threatening ecosystems by displacing native species, spreading diseases, and altering marine environments, with economic impacts on fisheries and power plant cooling systems, and billions in control costs. The Gulf’s high temperature and salinity levels favor hardy invaders. India and Singapore are highlighted as particularly vulnerable recipient regions. Estimates suggest each vessel may release millions of larvae into the Gulf during idle periods, enabling rapid dissemination via the international shipping network through hulls, ballast water, and onboard parasites and pathogens. Source: The Guardian report on a Biological Invasions study led by Mario Tamburri.

article.articleHeadline: Immune switch helps gut fight bacterial infections
article.articleSummary: Researchers in New Delhi, India, identify RelB as a key regulator of intestinal dendritic cells that orchestrate defense against bacterial infection. In a Citrobacter rodentium mouse model, deleting RelB in dendritic cells reduced IL-23 production, dampening IL-22–driven antimicrobial gene activation in the intestinal epithelium and increasing susceptibility to infection. The defect arises from RelB’s enhancement of Notch2 signaling, which supports a rare intestinal lymphoid tissue dendritic cell population that serves as the principal IL-23 source during infection. Restoring IL-23 in RelB-deficient mice reconstituted antibacterial immunity, confirming the pathway’s central role. The findings reveal a previously unrecognised RelB–Notch2 axis that links major immune signaling networks to gut defense and may inform therapies for intestinal infections and inflammatory bowel disease.

article.articleHeadline: Suspected patients arriving from Nepal-Uttarakhand will be monitored.
article.articleSummary: On July 29, 2026, PATH organized a workshop on identification and treatment of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis). Health officials were trained to identify, screen, and manage suspected kala-azar cases arriving from Nepal and Uttarakhand. Chaired by the Additional Director of Malaria and Vector-Borne Diseases and under the directive of the Additional Director of Health, officers from Bareilly, Badaun, Pilibhit, Shahjahanpur, Lakhimpur Kheri, Sambhal, and Rampur were briefed on surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment protocols for cases linked to cross-border or interstate movement. Kala-azar is caused by the parasite Leishmania donovani and spread by infected sandflies. The training emphasizes monitoring imported cases to prevent local transmission in these districts. Keywords: outbreak, surveillance, visceral leishmaniasis, cross-border, Nepal, Uttarakhand.

article.articleHeadline: Scientists detect that dengue-carrying mosquitoes are developing resistance to the most widely used insecticides, and warn that this could hinder disease control in the coming years.
article.articleSummary: Alpha-cypermethrin resistance detected in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in India threatens dengue and other arboviral disease control. Researchers from the University of Delhi report that two detoxification enzymes—beta-esterase and CYP450—enable survival against doses previously lethal. In controlled tests, a concentration once killing most exposed mosquitoes now eradicates about 97.71%, while 2.29% survive, signaling evolving resistance though not yet fully established. The beta-esterase activity increases up to 21-fold on exposure, aiding insecticide breakdown; CYP450 is also implicated in detoxification. The authors caution that resistance could spread regionally and complicate ongoing dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever programs unless surveillance and control strategies are adjusted. They propose rotating insecticides to recover efficacy, highlighting that real-time monitoring is essential since resistance timelines vary by region.

The free TB screening program is enabled by a memorandum of agreement between the Baguio City government and the Philippine Business for Social Progress (PBSP). The agreement, signed at City Hall by Mayor Benjamin Magalong, PBSP Executive Director Elvin Ivan Uy, and City Health Services Office Head Dr. Celia Flor Brillantes, aims to provide AI-powered TB screening for local residents and assist healthcare workers with rapid detection. article.articleHeadline: 3 bitten by rabid dog in Cotabato, prompting stray drive
article.articleSummary: Three people in Cotabato City, Philippines, were bitten by a rabid dog last Monday in Barangay Rosary Heights 2. Stray-dog capture has intensified, with dogs brought to the city dog pound in Barangay Rosary Heights 10. City officials are backtracking to locate the third bite victim so he can receive anti-rabies vaccine; the victims include a 53-year-old man and an 18-year-old female college student, both residents of Rosary Heights 2, and an adult male from General Santos City who worked as a mall delivery-truck employee. Residents are urged to seek immediate medical attention after any dog bite; early treatment is critical, and vaccines are reportedly sufficient. Hydrophobia signs may accompany rabies; reporting roaming strays is encouraged to prevent spread.

article.articleHeadline: DOH, ADB unveil ₱33.7-M infectious disease laboratory in Ilocos | Ma. Teresa Montemayor
article.articleSummary: In San Fernando City, Ilocos Region, DOH and the Ilocos Training and Regional Medical Center inaugurated a Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2) Infectious Disease Referral Laboratory. Built under the Health System Enhancement to Address and Limit (HEAL) Covid-19 Project and funded by the Asian Development Bank (ADB), it is one of only two BSL-2 labs nationwide under the program, which also funded 13 isolation wards. The US$125 million (≈P6.3 billion) ADB assistance package, approved in 2020, backs infrastructure, equipment, laboratory services, infection prevention, and workforce development. The facility, with a project cost of P33.69 million, will strengthen diagnostic capacity, disease surveillance, and rapid public health responses, enabling secure handling of infectious specimens and supporting timely clinical decisions to protect health security in the Ilocos Region and neighboring areas.

article.articleHeadline: 20 hogs culled over ASF
article.articleSummary: ASF outbreak in Cebu City, Philippines: 20 hogs culled after suspected infection; DVMF collected blood samples from the affected area, with the barangay identity not disclosed. Only one barangay was affected and Cebu City has since regained ASF-free status, though surveillance remains ongoing to prevent further spread. All affected hogs were culled and buried; the piggery was quarantined and its perimeter cordoned off as containment measures. Authorities extended assistance to the affected hog raiser, with financial aid from the DSWD being processed. African Swine Fever is a highly contagious viral disease affecting domestic and wild pigs; it poses no threat to humans but is often fatal to hogs, with mortality up to 100% in acute cases. Transmission occurs via direct contact, contaminated feed, vehicles, clothing, and ticks; there is no vaccine or cure, so biosecurity, culling, and movement restrictions are essential.

article.articleHeadline: A day in the life of Congo's overstretched Ebola surveillance teams
article.articleSummary: As of 29 July 2026, Bunia in the Democratic Republic of Congo remains the epicenter of an Ebola outbreak surging through the country. Surveillance teams, stretched thin, cope with limited transport: on a good day only four cars are available to cover 23 health districts serving about 1 million people. When Dr. Moubarack Kano arrived for duty, all four cars were out; he borrowed his own white Subaru Forester to chase emergency alerts with a colleague, emergency forms tucked in seat pockets, a rosary dangling from the rear-view mirror. The effort aims to trace infections and curb transmission across the city and surrounding districts. The account highlights the operational strain Ebola response faces in Bunia amid intensifying transmission and resource shortages.

At a July 28, 2026 press briefing in Kinshasa, Dr. De-Joseph Kakisingi M. stressed that defeating Ebola requires speed centered on communities, not only laboratories, treatment centers, or vaccines. Early analyses from Ituri and Tshopo indicate that distrust, rumors, communication gaps, and community engagement markedly influence spread and response timeliness. The approach supplements rather than replaces existing medical infrastructure, aiming to shorten delays between initial signs and control measures amid ongoing outbreaks and challenges such as strikes and misinformation.

article.articleHeadline: Conflicts can spread infectious diseases while making outbreaks harder to detect
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighboring Uganda may have caused deaths for weeks before alarm; Médecins Sans Frontières reports at least 55 deaths since early April 2026. On May 17, 2026, WHO declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern amid conflict that weakened clinics, laboratories and reporting. A broader analysis of WHO’s Disease Outbreak News (1996–2024) links armed conflict to both faster spread and reduced detection of infectious diseases, due to collapse of services and displacement. Polio outbreaks rise during civil wars from vaccination disruption; cholera outbreaks follow prolonged conflict as water and sanitation deteriorate, including Yemen’s record epidemic. Influenza was reported less often during conflict, possibly due to damaged labs and reporting. Patterns are strongest in sub-Saharan Africa, though data gaps and reporting inconsistencies limit causal conclusions about war and outbreak visibility.

article.articleHeadline: Monkeypox: What It Is, How It Is Transmitted, Symptoms, and How to Prevent It.
article.articleSummary: Monkeypox is an Orthopoxvirus infection. First identified in 1958 in monkeys in Denmark, the first human case was confirmed in 1970 in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). After a long African focus, a 2022 outbreak spread to Europe, the Americas, the Middle East, and Australia; as of July 2026, the DRC continues to face ongoing transmission. Two clades exist: Clade I (Central Africa, especially the DRC) with higher mortality, and Clade II (West Africa) generally milder. Transmission occurs via animal contact (bite, handling, bushmeat) and person-to-person through close contact, skin lesions, fluids, contaminated objects, droplets, and intimate contact including sex. Incubation 1–3 weeks; symptoms include vesicular-pustular rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, and respiratory symptoms; illness lasts 2–4 weeks. Diagnosis by PCR of lesion samples; no specific antiviral cure; supportive care. Prevention focuses on vaccination for high-risk exposures and hygiene; avoid contact with infected individuals and sharing personal items.

article.articleHeadline: COVID-19, Hantavirus and Ebola: What Has Changed?
article.articleSummary: Portugal remains without an integrated One Health strategy to address health threats, despite lessons from COVID-19. May, the Andes hantavirus outbreak concluded, exposed legal and institutional gaps in handling such events. The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, extending to Uganda and designated a WHO Public Health Emergency of International Concern, renewed alarms. Portuguese health authorities warned that there is no law enabling quarantine. Debates on an Emergency Health Protection Bill and constitutional revisions have stalled. With climate change likely increasing zoonotic spillovers, One Health remains theoretical rather than practiced across Health, Environment, and Agriculture. EU progress via HERA and cross-border threats regulation is uneven; IHR amendments took effect Sep 2025 and the Pandemic Treaty, adopted May 2025, awaits an annex and ratification. article.articleHeadline: From Prevention to Sovereignty: Accelerating Viral Hepatitis Elimination in Africa
article.articleSummary: As of 29 July 2026, 64 million Africans live with chronic hepatitis B; only 6% know their status and fewer than 2% receive treatment. Hepatitis B and C remain major killers, but elimination is achievable through scaled prevention, testing, and treatment within self-reliant health systems. Following the Cairo Declaration, the AU Plan toward eliminating vertical transmission by 2030 supports integrated maternal–newborn–child health services. Africa CDC’s Continental Viral Hepatitis Prevention and Control Programme coordinates regional action and launched an operational toolkit plus a decision-support platform translating WHO guidelines for frontline use. Birth-dose vaccination within 24 hours is at 17% of newborns; antenatal screening remains insufficient, leaving millions undiagnosed. Egypt’s 100 Million Healthier Lives, Rwanda’s screening, and Uganda’s HBV testing and monitoring illustrate progress; Nigeria, Senegal, Ghana, and Cameroon are advancing. Five priority areas: resilient primary health care, integrated surveillance and labs, predictable financing, digital transformation, and regional procurement and cooperation.

article.articleHeadline: The study: Ancient DNA reveals that the plague was killing people 5,500 years ago
article.articleSummary: Ancient plague (Yersinia pestis) DNA was found in 18 of 46 individuals from four hunter-gatherer cemeteries near Lake Baikal, eastern Siberia, dating to roughly 5,500 years ago, well before farming communities. By combining ancient genomes, archaeology, and radiocarbon dating, researchers describe short, intense mortality bursts, including graves with many children and youths. An ancient superantigen gene not present in later strains may drive strong inflammatory responses, making these early infections highly virulent even without flea-borne transmission. Radiocarbon results imply deaths occurred within a narrow window, sometimes among siblings or parent-child groups. The team suggests plague originated in Central or Northeast Asia and later spread across Eurasia via wild rodents, possibly transferring directly from infected marmots to humans. Published in Nature; the findings imply some of the earliest plagues were as deadly as later outbreaks, especially for children.
